public_rationale: Contemporary reporting directly records a Microsoft investor’s impatience with spending ahead of revenue. Microsoft’s earnings transcript also records scrutiny of the investment trajectory. Meta’s positive reception shows that investors were not uniformly rejecting AI spending. The ordinary claim of growing impatience is supported; a claim that all investors had lost confidence would not be.
limitations: The evidence establishes a visible concern, not a measured percentage of investors.
Market reactions also reflected company results and expectations beyond AI.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Investors are getting impatient with the AI boom and with the big tech companies funding it.

statement.excerpt: For reasons I’ve alluded to at the start of this article, investors are getting impatient with the AI hype boom — and, more specifically, with the giant tech companies that are bankrolling it.

from_speaker: with the giant tech companies that are bankrolling it
our_interpretation: The plain reading is a visible increase in investor concern about the time required for AI investments to produce returns, not unanimous rejection of AI.

Use July 2024 through August 5, covering the recent earnings discussions referenced in the post. Investor sentiment can be reported contemporaneously, so the target is the reporting window rather than the quarter whose earnings were released.
Share-price changes alone are insufficient; commentary must connect concern to AI spending or its expected payoff.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporary investor statements and earnings discussions show impatience about AI spending and delayed returns at major technology companies.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Broad contemporary evidence shows increasing investor patience with the AI investment cycle, while the cited negative reactions are attributable to unrelated matters.

evidence.excerpt: The street doesn't have a lot of patience.
evidence.locator: Quotation from Daniel Morgan, senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust
evidence.explanation: Morgan explicitly connects impatience to large expenditures and investors wanting corresponding revenue. Reuters identifies his firm as a Microsoft shareholder; no separate primary investor communication was located.

evidence.locator: Questions and answers, Kash Rangan of Goldman Sachs
evidence.explanation: The question is part of scrutiny of whether Microsoft could moderate spending while maintaining Azure and generative-AI growth. It corroborates concern but does not independently establish the prevalence of impatience.

evidence.locator: Reuters video transcript, concluding discussion of market reaction
evidence.explanation: Investors still rewarded a company reporting a reassuring outlook while investing in AI. This limits the breadth of the claim without refuting the existence of impatience elsewhere.
